opus-5.5.text:
I like to use the history of astronomy because it shows, step by step, how humans compressed the same phenomena into more and more compact symbolic forms. I usually describe it as roughly three or four levels.

The first level is just the raw data. Think of Tycho Brahe. He spent decades carefully recording the positions of planets night after night. That's an enormous table of numbers. It's accurate, but it isn't compressed at all. If you want to know where Mars will be, you basically look it up or interpolate. In machine learning terms, it's like memorizing the training set.

Before Kepler, there was also the Ptolemaic system with epicycles. People sometimes laugh at it, but I think it's an interesting intermediate stage. It's a model, and it predicts fairly well, but it's like a Fourier series: you keep adding circles on circles to fit the data. Today we'd call it a very flexible function approximator. It compresses a bit, but you need more parameters whenever you want more precision. That reminds me a lot of how neural networks often work. They fit very well, but the representation isn't necessarily the "true" one.

Then Kepler comes along, looks at Tycho's data, and finds three laws: elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the period squared proportional to the semi-major axis cubed. That's a huge jump in compression. A whole table of numbers becomes a few simple symbolic relations. But Kepler's laws are still phenomenological. They describe *what* happens, not *why*. And they're specific to planets orbiting the Sun.

Then Newton goes one level deeper. With F = ma and the inverse-square law of gravitation, you can *derive* Kepler's three laws. And the same equations explain the falling apple, the tides, and the Moon. So the compression is no longer only about this dataset. It generalizes across many seemingly unrelated phenomena. To me, that's the hallmark of a deeper level: fewer assumptions, broader coverage.

And of course you could keep going. Einstein's general relativity explains things Newton couldn't, like the precession of Mercury's perihelion, and it reframes gravity as geometry. Each step is a better compression of nature.

The reason I find this useful for AI is that it gives a concrete picture of what we want from "AI for science." Today's models are very good at the Tycho level, and even at the epicycle level: fitting data with a huge number of parameters. What's much harder is getting a model to make the Kepler jump, finding a compact, interpretable symbolic law. And the hardest is the Newton jump, finding the underlying principle that unifies many phenomena. That's partly what motivated work like KANs and our AI-physicist projects. We wanted to see whether we could design models whose internal structure is easier to compress into symbolic formulas, so that humans and AI can climb that ladder together instead of stopping at curve fitting.

So for me, astronomy is a nice ruler. When I look at a model, I ask: is this Tycho, is this Ptolemy, is this Kepler, or is this Newton?

r001.rationale: It says Kepler used Tycho’s data to find three laws, turning a whole table of observations into a few symbolic relations.

r002.rationale: It describes Newton’s laws of motion and inverse-square gravitation as a deeper compression that derives Kepler’s three laws.

fable-5.1.text:
I like to use astronomy because it's the cleanest example we have of science going through several stages of compression, each one a different kind of symbolic understanding.

The first stage is Tycho Brahe. He spent decades on an island just recording where the planets were, night after night. That's raw data. There's no compression yet, just a huge table of positions. But you can't skip this stage, because without good data nothing afterward is possible.

The second stage is Kepler. He stared at Tycho's tables and found that the orbit of Mars was an ellipse, that planets sweep out equal areas in equal times, that the period squared goes with the radius cubed. Those three laws compress the entire table into a few formulas. That's what I'd call phenomenological or empirical compression. You've found the pattern, you can predict, but you don't really know why. Kepler himself was confused about the why; he had all sorts of ideas about magnetism and divine geometry.

The third stage is Newton. He said: all of Kepler's laws are consequences of one thing, the inverse-square law of gravitation plus F equals ma. Now the three laws become one principle, and the same principle also explains apples falling and tides. This is a much deeper level of compression, because it's not just compressing the data of planetary motion, it's compressing many seemingly unrelated phenomena into a single mechanism.

And then you can go further. Einstein compressed Newton again: gravity isn't a force, it's the geometry of spacetime. Each step, the description gets shorter and the explanatory range gets wider.

The reason I care about this is that it maps very well onto what we try to do with AI for science, and onto what I think about with symbolic regression and things like KANs. When a neural network fits data, it's a bit like Tycho's table in a different form: a lot of parameters, high accuracy, no understanding. When you extract a compact formula from it, you've reached the Kepler level. That's already valuable, and honestly most of what current symbolic methods can do is at that level. But what scientists really want is the Newton level, where the formula is derived from a principle, where you understand why. And I think the hard, interesting question right now is whether machines can make that jump from Kepler to Newton, from finding patterns to finding the mechanism that generates the patterns.

So when I talk about levels of compression, I'm really using astronomy as a ladder. It tells you where a given method sits, and it also tells you honestly how far we still have to climb.

r001.rationale: It says Kepler’s three laws compress Tycho’s tables of planetary positions into a few formulas.

r002.rationale: It says Newton’s inverse-square gravitation and F = ma make Kepler’s three laws consequences of one principle.

astra-6.text:
I think the history of astronomy gives us a nice example of how the same observations can be compressed at different levels. At the first level, you have a record of where the planets appear in the sky. You can think of that as a big table: each entry tells you a position at a particular time.

Then Kepler’s laws compress those observations into a few mathematical relationships. Instead of storing all the positions, you describe an elliptical orbit and how the planet moves along it. That is already a huge reduction in the amount of information you need.

Newton gives you another level of compression. His laws of motion and universal gravitation explain Kepler’s laws, and they also describe falling objects on Earth. So you are compressing several apparently different phenomena into one framework. You still need initial conditions to predict a particular orbit, but the underlying rule is shared.

The distinction I would make is between compressing observations into patterns and compressing those patterns into a more general theory. A deeper theory is powerful because it does more than summarize what you have already seen: it also constrains what you should expect to see next.

r001.rationale: The response says Kepler’s laws compress astronomical position observations, but it does not identify those observations as Tycho’s.

r002.rationale: It presents Newton’s laws of motion and universal gravitation as a further level that explains Kepler’s laws and unifies them with falling objects on Earth.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the history of astronomy gives us a nice example of successive levels of symbolic compression. You start with observations: where the planets appear in the sky at different times. That’s a large amount of data. Then you look for a compact representation of those observations.

One level is to describe the apparent motion using circles and epicycles. You’re compressing the observations into a mathematical model that can predict positions. Then Kepler’s laws give you another representation: planets move in ellipses, sweep out equal areas in equal times, and follow a relationship between orbital period and orbital size. A lot of observational detail becomes a few regularities.

Newton takes that further. Instead of treating those regularities as separate facts about planets, you can derive them from laws of motion and universal gravitation. The same framework also describes a falling object on Earth. So the compression is deeper because it connects phenomena that previously looked different.

The distinction I would make is between compressing data into patterns and compressing patterns into a shared principle. And compression doesn’t mean simply writing fewer symbols. You want a compact description that preserves predictive power—and ideally tells you something beyond the observations you started with.

r001.rationale: The response describes Kepler’s laws as summarizing astronomical observations, but it does not identify those observations as Tycho’s.

r002.rationale: It says Newton derives the Keplerian regularities from laws of motion and universal gravitation, presenting that framework as a deeper compression.
